MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you read a post-op THA film?"
- "Six fixed steps: cup **inclination**, cup **offset**, **stem position**, **leg length**, femoral **offset**, **fixation by zones**."
- "Targets: inclination 30–50°, **Lewinnek 40 ± 10°**, anteversion **15 ± 10°**, stem central."
- "Compare with the **immediate post-op film**: change over time beats any single number."

### The Six Steps
Each step answers one question, always in the same order.

#### Films Required
- At every visit, inspect four things: components, cement, bone and their **interfaces**
- The AP and the lateral must show the **whole stem**, compared with earlier films
- Standard set: **AP pelvis** + **cross-table lateral**
- **CT** when the version of either component is in doubt
- The recovery-room AP and lateral are the **baseline** film

#### Order of Reading
| Step | Parameter | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cup **inclination** | **theta angle** 30–50° |
| 2 | Cup **offset** | hip centre → teardrop plane |
| 3 | **Stem position** | tip-to-cortex distance |
| 4 | **LLD** (leg-length discrepancy) | inter-teardrop line → lesser trochanter |
| 5 | Femoral **offset** | hip centre → medullary axis |
| 6 | **Fixation by zones** | mantle and interfaces: Gruen (femur) · DeLee–Charnley (cup) |

- Steps 1 and 2 read the cup, so they apply to a **THA only**, not a hemiarthroplasty
- Read the cup in order: inclination, version, height and depth, then a centred head
- Step 6 is the **cement mantle** in a cemented hip; in a cementless hip it is the interfaces

#### Why a Fixed Order
- A fixed order stops you halting at the first finding
- It mirrors planning: the cup first, then the stem, then the result
- The first film is the baseline, so every later film is compared with it

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Theta → cup offset → stem tip → LLD → femoral offset → zones · lateral tip = varus = no**

MEMORY HOOK — the house inspector
- Inspect it like a house: the roof (cup), the pillar (stem), the level floor (leg length), then the cracks (zones).

6.2.b:
The cup is read first: its tilt, its facing and its depth.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "is this cup well placed?"
- "Inclination by the **theta angle**: accept **30–50°**."
- "Version is only estimated on the AP: confirm on a **cross-table lateral**, measure on **CT**."
- "Cup offset should restore the **centre of rotation**, neither lateral nor medial."

### Inclination: The Theta Angle
Inclination is how steeply the cup opens on the AP film.

#### Measurement
- **Theta** is the angle between the cup face and a horizontal line
- The horizontal is the **interischial** or the **inter-teardrop** line
- The accepted range is **30–50°**; the cup is templated at **45°** (Handbook)
- A pelvis tilted or rotated to the beam distorts the angle
- Measure both hips on the same horizontal line → 13 a06

#### Outside the Range
- Too steep means **edge loading** and wear
- In metal-on-metal bearings, a steep cup also releases **metal ions**
- Too flat means impingement early in **flexion**, so the hip dislocates **posteriorly**
- Low anteversion makes the flat cup worse
- Look for bone or cement left beyond the cup face: it is a fulcrum for dislocation
- Which way each extreme dislocates → 13 Instability

### Version
Version is which way the cup faces, and the AP film only hints at it.

#### Measurement
- On the AP, superimposed cup margins mean little or no version
- An **ellipse** means some version, but the AP cannot tell ante- from **retroversion**
- The **cross-table lateral** shows the direction
- In a cemented cup, the marker wire's two halves give version by calculation (**McLaren**)
- The wire also shows cup position, wear and cement thickness
- **CT** is the most accurate: a cup normal on the AP was **20°** retroverted (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 6.1 · 6.2
- CT finds malposition missed on films; a component **>10°** off is revised (Prof Azzam)

#### Comparing Films
- Compare only **rotationally identical** films: match the obturator foramina and pelvic outline
- Pelvic rotation changes the apparent anteversion; inclination changes little

#### The Direct Anterior Approach
- With the **DAA** (direct anterior approach), set anteversion **15°** from the floor (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Set inclination at **40°**: he places most of his cups there
[[FIG: Fig 6.2 · 6.2
- Supine, the cup tends to drift into excess **abduction** and **anteversion**
- So fluoroscopy checks reaming and cup position

### Lewinnek Safe Zone
The safe zone joins tilt and facing into one target box.
- Inclination **40 ± 10°**, so 30–50°, the same range as theta
- Anteversion **15 ± 10°**, so 5–25° (Campbell; Prof Azzam)
- Judge each angle alone: a **60°** cup is too steep even with 15–20° anteversion
- Why a cup outside it dislocates, and why some inside it still do → 13 Instability
- Redefined zones and spinopelvic targets → 13 Instability

PITFALL — 40°, 45° or 30–50°?
- Theta 30–50° and template 45° (Handbook); Lewinnek 40 ± 10°; his routine cup 40°
- In theatre Campbell aims **40–45°** inclination and **20–25°** anteversion
- Say → "**accept 30–50°, aim near 40°** (Lewinnek 40 ± 10°); the Handbook templates at 45°"

MEMORY HOOK — forty tilts, fifteen faces
- **Forty tilts, fifteen faces**, and ten forgives either way: Lewinnek 40 ± 10°, 15 ± 10°.

### Acetabular Offset
Cup offset tells you how deep the cup sits.

#### Definition
- Measure from the hip centre to the **teardrop plane**, on both sides
- Equal on both sides means neither medialised nor lateralised
- Longer than the other side means **lateralised**
- Shorter means **medialised**
- The hip centre is set by vertical offset, horizontal offset and version

#### Centre of Rotation
- The cup centre should sit at the **teardrop**, where the ilio-ischial and ilio-pubic lines meet
- Its height and depth should match the other hip
- A slightly **high hip centre** is a finding to report
- Restoring a high centre is the **long-term** goal: a normal JRF, so less wear and loosening
- The **Ranawat** method finds the true centre from the Köhler and Shenton lines, useful in protrusio
- The **teardrop** is the fixed landmark for cup position on serial films
[[FIG: Fig 6.3 · 6.2
- High-riding hips: cups go back to the true acetabulum
[[FIG: Fig 6.4 · 6.2
- Drawing of horizontal and vertical centre restoration → 03 Hip biomechanics

#### Effect on Hip Mechanics
- Medialising shortens the body-weight lever, so joint load falls
- But it also slackens the **abductors**; lateralising does the reverse
- The goal is neither: restore the **centre of rotation** (Prof Fawzy)
- In dysplasia, restore the centre first, so the cup is stable now and later
- A high-profile cemented cup lateralises the centre slightly; a low-profile cup medialises it
- The levers themselves → 03 Hip biomechanics

#### Two Limits
- Over-reaming medially breaches the **medial wall**, so the teardrop is the limit
- If cup offset is lost, add **femoral offset**, so the abductors stay tensioned

### Cemented Cup Fixation
A cemented cup shows its mantle and its wire on the first film.
- The cup mantle is ≈**3 mm**, kept even by 3 mm PMMA spacers; the course says 2–4 mm (→ 02)
- Spacers and marker wire → 02 Fixation & cement

6.3.b:
Then the stem: where its tip sits, how it is fixed, and how far it holds the femur from the hip centre.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "is this stem well placed?"
- "A **central** tip is normal; a **lateral** tip means **varus**: not accepted."
- "A **medial** tip means **valgus**: accepted, but it costs offset."
- "**Femoral offset** is hip centre to shaft axis; imitate the patient's own."

### Stem Position
The tip-to-cortex gaps tell you the stem's alignment.

#### Reading the Tip
| Tip | Means | Verdict (Handbook) |
|---|---|---|
| **Central** | equal gaps both sides | normal |
| **Lateral tip** (less lateral gap) | **varus**: lateral bending, instability, loosening, fracture | **not accepted** |
| **Medial tip** (less medial gap) | **valgus** | accepted |

#### Consequences of Varus and Valgus
- Varus gives a longer lever, so cemented stems crack and loosen
- A varus cementless stem is undersized and subsides early
- **Varus** means more offset and a shorter leg
[[FIG: Fig 6.5 · 6.3
- **Valgus** means less offset and a longer leg

#### Cause and Prevention of Varus
- Varus usually comes from an **entry point too medial**
- So start toward the **greater trochanter** before broaching

#### Comparing Both Sides
- Compare the **medial (femoral) offset** with the other side
- Compare the **vertical offset** too: hip centre to the top of the lesser trochanter
- Femoral version does not show on the AP; CT measures it with the cup

#### After Previous Fixation
- A long stem must pass the last screw hole by **2 cortical diameters** (Prof Gobba)
- Planning around old hardware → 05 Planning

PITFALL — "lateral tip": good or bad?
- The tip touches the lateral cortex because the stem leans into varus
- The tip goes lateral, so the neck drops and the neck–shaft angle falls
- Say → "**lateral tip = varus = not accepted; medial tip = valgus = accepted**"

MEMORY HOOK — the leaning tower
- A varus stem is a leaning tower: its tip leans on the lateral wall, and it cracks or loosens.

### Femoral Offset
Femoral offset is the abductors' lever arm, so the film checks it was kept.

#### Definition
- **Femoral (medial) offset** is the distance from hip centre to femoral shaft axis
[[FIG: Fig 6.6 · 6.3
- It continues the acetabular offset laterally
- The Handbook names four offsets: acetabular, femoral, vertical and "anteversion"
- The film reads the two horizontal ones and the vertical one
- Against the other side: equal is normal; greater is increased; smaller is decreased
- Its role as the abductor lever, and too little or too much → 03 Hip biomechanics

#### Restoring It
- Always **imitate** the patient's own offset (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Length need not match if the other hip is diseased
- A **high-offset** (lateralised) stem restores offset without lengthening
- Its head moves medially, not up
- On trial, a distal pull tests vertical offset; a lateral pull tests lateral offset
- A femur that pulls out laterally needs an extended-offset stem
- Unseen loss of offset is often "corrected" by **overlengthening**
- A long neck with high offset can impinge and lever out → 13 Instability

### Fixation on the Immediate Film
The first film also shows how well the stem was fixed.

#### Cemented Stem
- The stem should be central, with a mantle ≈**4 mm** proximal and **2 mm** distal
- The stem fills about **80%** of the canal (Campbell)
- The stem tip should rest on cement, because the tip takes axial load
- Grade the mantle by **Barrack** A–D; grades C and D loosen more
- Barrack table → 02 Fixation & cement

#### Polished Taper
- A **void below the tip** is planned (hollow centraliser), so the stem can subside
- A bonded stem must have no void; there it is a Barrack D defect
- Taper subsidence in its mantle → 02 Fixation & cement

#### Cementless Stem
- Judge **fit and fill** on both the AP and the lateral
- A double-wedge stem fills the metaphysis in both planes
- A big canal-filling stem is stiffer (stiffness ∝ diameter⁴), so expect more stress shielding
- A collar spreads load and lessens proximal stress shielding
- A few loose beads on the first film come from impaction
- Beads shed **progressively** on later films mean micromotion

6.4.b:
The fourth step asks whether the planned length came true.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you check leg length after THA?"
- "One line across the teardrops; measure to the **top of each lesser trochanter**."
- "Control length in theatre: square pelvis, pins, rulers, trial films."
- "Once healed, a **shoe raise** is usually all that is left."

### Measurement on the Film
The same line used in planning now checks the result.
- Draw the **inter-teardrop line**, and measure to the top of each **lesser trochanter**
- The interischial line also works; the teardrop is more accurate
- Then ask: was the pre-operative LLD corrected?
- Example: 2.5 cm before surgery, 3 mm after, so not significant (Handbook)
- A clear difference means the neck cut, stem seating or cup height changed
- So tell the patient early
- In an unacceptable LLD, look for an **inferior cup** or, more often, a **proud stem**
- Take full-length films for causes outside the hip
- An oversized cup lowers the hip centre and lengthens the leg **1 cm** (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 6.7 · 6.4
- A high femoral cortical index tends to lengthen; a low one to shorten
[[FIG: Fig 6.8 · 6.4
- Feeling and film differ: **30%** felt an LLD, and only **36%** of them had one (Campbell)
- Lesser-trochanter line after revision → 04 a12
- Pre-operative LLD and its limits → 05 Planning

### Intraoperative Control
Length is cheap to fix in theatre and costly afterwards (Prof Fawzy).

#### Priorities
- The priorities are pain relief, stability, mobility, then equal length
- So warn before surgery that stability may need some lengthening
- An LLD can be minimised, not abolished

#### Positioning Checks
- Supine: keep the pelvis **square**, with the medial malleoli level
[[FIG: Fig 6.9 · 6.4
- Lateral: use traction, soft-tissue tension and the **knee-flexion test**
- Traction separation depends on the pull, relaxation and capsule release
- The lateral approach detaches more abductors, so it separates more
- A normal shuck is **2–4 mm** with the hip extended (Campbell)
- Soft-tissue tension alone must not decide length
- Do the knee-flexion test with the hip extended
- If the flexed leg kicks back, it is too long

#### Measuring Devices
- A **Steinmann pin** in the ilium measures to the greater trochanter tip
[[FIG: Fig 6.10 · 6.4
- Read it again after trial reduction
- The pin must be rigid, and the limb back in the same position
- Ranawat pin method: mean LLD **1.9 mm** (Campbell)
- A caliper jig reads length and offset together
- Navigation and an X-ray on trial reduction are alternatives
- Navigation is more accurate for length, but not better clinically, and costs time
- Templating plus intra-op measuring works: **92%** within **5 mm** of plan (Campbell)
- Only **2.5%** were lengthened more than **6 mm** with this approach
- Posterior or lateral approach: **Schanz pin** and sterile ruler; to lengthen 2 cm, go from 9 to 11 cm (Prof Sherif Khaled)

#### Intra-operative Films
- Seat the smallest reamer at the planned centre and take an image-intensifier shot
- Correct a high or medial position before the cup goes in
- Fluoroscopy trials are mixed: fewer LLD over **1 cm**, but no clear gain in cup position
- With the DAA and fluoroscopy, one series had no cup steeper than **55°**
- It helps only when pelvic tilt and rotation are controlled

#### The Direct Anterior Approach
- The DAA allows a direct view and the **Galeazzi** test
- Compare the medial malleoli; do Galeazzi with hips and knees at **45°** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- A traction table with both feet in boots makes this comparison harder

PITFALL — the wrong place for a surprise
- Never ream, insert the cup, and only then find the wrong position on the film
- Say → "**check with the smallest reamer and an image before the cup**"

### Established Discrepancy
After surgery the options shrink.
- Too late, only a **shoe raise** remains (Prof Fawzy)
- Early felt lengthening, limits and revision indications → 05 Planning

MEMORY HOOK — the cobbler
- Measure twice in theatre, because after surgery the only surgeon left is the cobbler (shoe raise).

- Navigation and an X-ray on trial reduction are alternatives
- Navigation is more accurate for length, but not better clinically, and costs time
- Templating plus intra-op measuring works: **92%** within **5 mm** of plan (Campbell)
- Only **2.5%** were lengthened more than **6 mm** with this approach
- Posterior or lateral approach: **Schanz pin** and sterile ruler; to lengthen 2 cm, go from 9 to 11 cm (Prof Sherif Khaled)

#### Intra-operative Films
- Seat the smallest reamer at the planned centre and take an image-intensifier shot
- Correct a high or medial position before the cup goes in
- Fluoroscopy trials are mixed: fewer LLD over **1 cm**, but no clear gain in cup position
- With the DAA and fluoroscopy, one series had no cup steeper than **55°**
- It helps only when pelvic tilt and rotation are controlled

#### The Direct Anterior Approach
- The DAA allows a direct view and the **Galeazzi** test
- Compare the medial malleoli; do Galeazzi with hips and knees at **45°** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- A traction table with both feet in boots makes this comparison harder

PITFALL — the wrong place for a surprise
- Never ream, insert the cup, and only then find the wrong position on the film
- Say → "**check with the smallest reamer and an image before the cup**"

6.4.3.b:
After surgery the options shrink.
- Too late, only a **shoe raise** remains (Prof Fawzy)
- Early felt lengthening, limits and revision indications → 05 Planning

MEMORY HOOK — the cobbler
- Measure twice in theatre, because after surgery the only surgeon left is the cobbler (shoe raise).

6.5.b:
The last step maps the bone–implant border, so changes can be named by zone.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you describe a lucency?"
- "Femur: **Gruen 7 zones** on the AP, **14** with the lateral."
- "Cup: **DeLee–Charnley 3 zones**."
- "A lucency **spreading zone to zone** on serial films means loosening."

Gruen zones circle the femoral stem.

#### Numbering on the AP Film
| Zone | Gruen (femur) |
|---|---|
| 1 · 2 · 3 | upper · middle · lower ⅓ lateral |
| 4 | below the stem tip |
| 5 · 6 · 7 | lower · middle · upper ⅓ medial |

- Zone 1 is the lateral shoulder; zone 7 is the **calcar**

#### Lateral Film
- On the lateral film Gruen has **14 zones** (Prof Fahmy)
- Zones 8–14 cover the anterior and posterior surfaces

MEMORY HOOK — the round trip
- Gruen takes a round trip: down the lateral side (1–3), round the tip (4), up the medial side (5–7).

### DeLee–Charnley Zones
The cup has 3 zones, numbered lateral to medial.

| Zone | DeLee–Charnley (cup) |
|---|---|
| 1 | superolateral |
| 2 | central |
| 3 | inferomedial |

- Draw a vertical and a horizontal line through the cup centre
- Lateral to the vertical line is 1; below the horizontal line is 3; between is 2

### Serial Interpretation
One film shows a line; a series shows a process.

#### Technique
- Use the same technique and limb position each time
- **10°** of limb rotation can fake, or hide, stem migration (Campbell)
- Record the zones where anything changes, at every visit

#### Schedule
- Films yearly at first, then every **3**, then every **3–5** years (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Cup loosening is often painless, so follow-up films are not optional
- Once osteolysis is seen, film every **6–12 months** (Campbell)

#### Signs of Change
- A lucency spreading from zone to zone on **serial films** means loosening
- One image alone is not enough
- A cemented cup with a lucency **≥2 mm** in all three zones is loose (Campbell)
- Its extent matters more than its width
- A change in cup inclination or version on serial films is definite loosening
- Subsidence is measured from a fixed point on the stem to the trochanter or a wire
- A polished taper subsides about **1 mm** in the first year, by design (Prof Hazem)
- Early cementless settling may stabilise; late subsidence means instability
- Loosening signs and radiolucency grading → 11 Painful arthroplasty
- Gruen's modes of stem failure and subsidence limits → 14 Loosening
